questions.prompt: Why load a CS stage with a current source instead of a resistor?
options: It gives a large small-signal resistance with only a small DC voltage drop
It makes the gain independent of \(g_m\)
It removes the need for a supply
questions.explanation: A resistor large enough for high gain would drop more than the supply; a saturated PMOS needs only \(|V_{ov}|\) of headroom.

questions.explanation: Each device needs its own overdrive across it to stay saturated (reader Sec. 13.2.2).

questions.prompt: To match the load resistance of a 50 kΩ \(r_o\) with a resistor at \(I_D = 100\ \mu\mathrm{A}\), how much DC voltage (V) would that resistor drop?
questions.explanation: \(100\ \mu\mathrm{A}\times50\ \mathrm{k\Omega} = 5\ \mathrm{V}\), more than a modern supply. The current source gives the same small-signal resistance across a fraction of a volt.

questions.prompt: With matched \(\lambda\) and fixed \(V_{ov}\), you halve the bias current of a current-source-loaded CS stage. What happens to the gain?
questions.explanation: \(|A_v| = 2/[V_{ov}(\lambda_n + \lambda_p)]\) has no current in it. Lower current costs speed, not gain.
